title: The Order
full_review:
A maverick Catholic priest becomes entangled in a bizarre web of occult ritualism and shadowy Vatican intrigue in the execrable supernatural thriller "The Order" (20th Century Fox). Wrapped in a convoluted story, director Brian Helgeland's film is full of egregious theological distortions and bogus stereotypes, targeted at painting the church and its clergy as callous, corrupt and ultimately faithless.

The pretzel of a plot revolves around an arcane medieval ritual known as "sin eating," a heretical -- and fatal -- rite by which initiates claimed they could absolve the dying of their wrongdoings by placing bread and salt on the penitent's body and literally consuming their transgressions, along with the knowledge of their sinful acts.

The messy affair is set in motion when the elderly head of a fictitious priestly order called the Carolingians, Father Dominic (Francesco Carnelutti), excommunicated some years earlier for "delving deep and dark" after esoteric knowledge, dies in Rome under mysterious circumstances. The death is labeled a suicide by the ecclesiastical authorities, though clues point to ritual murder.

Hearing of his mentor's passing, Dominic's young protege, Father Alex Bernier (Heath Ledger), a New York cleric grappling with a "Thorn Birds"-esque dark night of the soul, hops a jet to Rome, accompanied by a psychologically disturbed artist, Mara (Shannyn Sossamon), for whom he harbors romantic feelings. In one of the many story lines never fully explained, it is revealed that Bernier had previously performed an exorcism on Mara during which she had tried to kill him, though it remains up in the air whether she was actually ever really possessed or merely a garden-variety mental case.

Once in the Eternal City, Bernier uncovers the fact that his teacher had enlisted the services of a "sin eater" as an alternative to the sacramental absolution denied him by his excommunication. The Vatican, a favorite whipping boy of Hollywood, shrugs off the rogue priest's findings about his already ecclesiastically discredited mentor. Having exhausted all official channels, Bernier, along with fellow Carolingian Father Thomas Garret (Mark Addy), a burly, heterodox Irishman, descends into Rome's murky underbelly -- including a subterranean S&M bar patronized by transvestite clerics and profanely adorned with holy symbols -- in order to track down Dominic's killer.

Weaving their way through a thicket of plot twists, their search leads them to an enigmatic figure called William Eden (Benno Furmann), who learned the black arts in his youth during the 15th century, and, having not aged in the ensuing 500 years, has marked Bernier as his likely successor.

Complicating the already labyrinthine narrative is a subplot revolving around a shady would-be pope, Cardinal Driscoll (Peter Weller), who is involved in an unholy cabalistic conspiracy to usurp the papacy.

Beyond its innumerable theological misrepresentations, the film is weighed down by a cipher of a script, containing a vortex of muddled narrative threads, which Helgeland seems unable to channel into a cohesive story. Ledger sulks through the movie with all the charisma of a wet blanket.

While its moodiness does intone a sepulchral otherworldly milieu, "The Order's" supernatural effects are as laughable as they are theologically unsound. In the scenes depicting the sin-eating ceremony, the penitent's sins rise out of their chests in the form of ghostly jellyfish. The film's sole other attempt at demonic creepiness involves a tag team of two hell-spawn children who attack Bernier in a graveyard -- a scene which serves no purpose beyond TV ad fodder.

The film leaves no anti-church cliche unturned, citing the usual trumped up charges of repression, hypocrisy and cruelty. Locked in Helgeland's crosshairs, church hierarchs are caricatured as intolerant careerists, with several priestly figures presented as depraved blasphemers. Even God does not escape Helgeland's vitriolic cynicism, as Eden derisively opines that while he exists "(God) just doesn't give a damn."

Chastity is mocked throughout, and much of the dialogue amounts to little more than a tired polemic against celibacy, demanding sexual activity as a prerequisite for manhood. In one scene Garret chides Bernier for not sleeping with Mara, saying, "You're a priest sleeping on the couch, rather than a man sleeping in a bed with a woman." Of course, by the film's end such trivialities as vows are dispensed with as Bernier has sex with Mara in room full of sacred icons, deeming himself afterward, by fiat, no longer a priest -- yet another illustration of Helgeland's erroneous grasp of the Catholic understanding of sacramental life.

Equally offensive is the film's portrayal of the church as a hardhearted dispenser of God's mercy, dangling it like a carrot over humanity, quick to withhold it for the slightest infraction -- the film suggests that the church would have disapproved of Christ forgiving the good thief on the cross because he was a criminal. While remaining the story's villain, it is Eden, not the church, who comes off as the font of clemency, bestowing, without judgment, get-out-of-hell-free cards for the right price -- a perverse understanding of forgiveness that turns absolution into a parlor magic trick and strips it of the element of contrition.

Perhaps most pernicious is the film's attempt to put faith and truth at odds, going so far at one point as stating that "knowledge is the enemy of faith," a dangerous stance refuted by Pope John Paul II's eloquent encyclical, "Fides et Ratio," a defense of both faith and reason in which he describes them not as sparring partners but as "two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of the truth."

Due to a warped view of church doctrine, a shadowy sexual encounter with partial nudity, a suicide, recurring violence including ritual murder, and sporadic rough and crude language, as well as profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
